hints: Start from the total electrons in Cu (29) and recall why Cu does not follow the expected $3d^9 4s^2$ pattern, think about the stability of a full $3d$ subshell.
When Cu forms $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, decide which subshell loses electrons first, the $4s$ or the $3d$, and count how many electrons remain in $3d$.
walkthrough:
Sort out neutral Cu first**
You know Cu has 29 electrons, so after $[\text{Ar}]$ (18) you have 11 left. You might expect $3d^9 4s^2$, but a completely full $3d^{10}$ with a half filled $4s^1$ is lower in energy. So picture all five $3d$ boxes full with paired arrows, and the $4s$ box holding just one electron.

Remove electrons to make Cu2+ correctly**
A very common slip is to take electrons from $3d$ first. Always take from the highest principal quantum number first, so both electrons come from $4s$ and $3d$. The $4s^1$ electron is lost, plus one $3d$ electron. That leaves $3d^9$ and an empty $4s$. In boxes that is four full pairs plus one single electron in $3d$.

Final answer: Cu: $[\text{Ar}]$ $3d^{10}$ $4s^1$, five $3d$ boxes all paired ($\uparrow\downarrow$ in each) and $4s$ box with one $\uparrow$ electron.
$\text{Cu}^{2+}$: $[\text{Ar}]$ $3d^9$, four $3d$ boxes paired and one box with single $\uparrow$ electron, $4s$ box empty.

hints: Look at the diagram for the isolated $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ion where all five $3d$ boxes are drawn at exactly the same height on the energy axis.
walkthrough:
Read degenerate as an energy word**
In an isolated gaseous ion there is nothing around to disturb the $d$ electrons differently. All five $3d$ orbitals feel the same environment, so they sit on one common energy level. That is all degenerate means here, same energy.
Final answer: Degenerate means the (five $3d$) orbitals have the same energy.

hints: Think about what changes when six ligands approach along the x, y and z axes, some $d$ orbitals point directly at ligands while others point between them.
walkthrough:
See why the single level splits**
Put six ligands around $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ in an octahedron. Two $d$ orbitals ($d_{z^2}$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$) point straight at the ligands, so electrons in them are repelled more and pushed up in energy. The other three ($d_{xy}$, $d_{xz}$, $d_{yz}$) point between ligands, so they are repelled less and drop down. You draw this as a small gap, 2 boxes up, 3 boxes down.
Final answer: In octahedral complex $3d$ orbitals split into two sets: upper set of 2 boxes ($e_g$) and lower set of 3 boxes ($t_{2g}$) at higher and lower energy than the isolated ion level.

hints: Break the word bidentate into bi meaning two, and think about what a ligand uses to bond to the metal, its lone pairs on N.
walkthrough:
Link the two N atoms to two bonds**
Look at $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. Each N has a lone pair that can form a coordinate bond to $\text{Cu}^{2+}$. Because one $en$ molecule uses both N atoms to bond at the same time, it donates two electron pairs in total. That two point attachment is exactly what bidentate describes.
Final answer: A bidentate ligand is an ion or molecule that donates two pairs of electrons (forms two coordinate bonds) to the central metal ion.

hints: Count the bonds needed, an octahedral Cu needs six donor atoms, each $en$ provides two N donors, so three $en$ units wrap around Cu joining adjacent (cis) positions.
Imagine the three chelate rings as blades of a propeller, think how you could arrange them clockwise in one complex and anticlockwise in the other to make a pair of mirror images.
walkthrough:
Build one correct octahedral unit**
Place Cu in the centre with six octahedral directions. Each $en$ must join two neighbouring positions, not opposite positions, because the short $\text{N-C-C-N}$ chain can only bite at about 90 degrees. With three $en$ ligands you fill all six sites, forming three chelate rings around Cu.

Create the mirror image pair**
Now think in 3D. The three rings can twist like a propeller in two opposite senses. Draw the second structure as the exact mirror image of the first, swapping left and right, wedges and dashes. The two drawings cannot be superimposed, so they are the pair of optical isomers of $[\text{Cu}(en)_3]^{2+}$.

Final answer: Draw $[\text{Cu}(en)_3]^{2+}$ as octahedral Cu with three $en$ ligands each spanning two cis positions.
Draw two structures that are non-superimposable mirror images (delta and lambda optical isomers).
